The '''61st Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), honored the best [[1988 in film|films of 1988]] and took place on March 29, 1989, at the [[Shrine Auditorium]] in Los Angeles, beginning at 6:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]]&nbsp;/ 9:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]].<ref name="TMS">{{harvnb|Osborne|2008|p=296}}</ref> During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 23 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Allan Carr]] and directed by [[Jeff Margolis]].<ref name="TMS"/> Ten days earlier, in a ceremony held at the [[Beverly Hills Hotel]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], the [[Academy Award for Technical Achievement|Academy Awards for Technical Achievement]] were presented by host [[Angie Dickinson]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013 |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

''[[Rain Man]]'' won four awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]]. Other winners included ''[[Who Framed Roger Rabbit]]'' with four awards, ''[[Dangerous Liaisons]]'' with three, and ''[[The Accused (1988 film)|The Accused]]'', ''[[The Accidental Tourist (film)|The Accidental Tourist]]'', ''[[A Fish Called Wanda]]'', ''[[The Appointments of Dennis Jennings]]'', ''[[Beetlejuice]]'', ''[[Bird (1988 film)|Bird]]'', ''[[Hôtel Terminus: The Life and Times of Klaus Barbie]]'', ''[[The Milagro Beanfield War]]'', ''[[Mississippi Burning]]'', ''[[Pelle the Conqueror]]'', ''[[Tin Toy]]'', ''[[Working Girl]]'', and ''[[You Don't Have to Die]]'' with one award each.

The telecast drew in over 42 million viewers in the United States, making it the most-viewed ceremony up to that point, until it was surpassed by the [[70th Academy Awards]] in 1998, which garnered a viewership of over 57 million.<ref name="Oscar ratings" /><ref name="SnowJob" /> The ceremony featured changes such as the introduction of the phrase "And the Oscar goes to..." and the absence of a traditional host. The ceremony's opening number, featuring [[Snow White]] and [[Rob Lowe]], received heavy criticism. Allan Carr faced significant backlash, leading the Academy to form a committee to address the criticisms and evaluate the ceremony's production.

== Winners and nominees ==
The nominees for the 61st Academy Awards were announced on February 15, 1989, at the [[Samuel Goldwyn Theater]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], by Richard Kahn, president of the Academy, and actress [[Anne Archer]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Williams|first=Jeannie |title= Michael's high-profile feast|work=[[USA Today]] |page=2D|date=February 16, 1989|df=mdy-all}}</ref> ''[[Rain Man]]'' led all nominees, with eight; ''[[Dangerous Liaisons]]'' and ''[[Mississippi Burning]]'' tied for second with seven each.<ref>{{cite news|last=Cieply |first=Michael |title='Rain Man' Given 8 Oscar Nominations; Sigourney 2 : Hoffman Wins 6th Acting Nod |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-02-15-mn-2644-story.html |access-date= October 4, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=February 16, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131004232746/http://articles.latimes.com/1989-02-15/news/mn-2644_1_rain-man |archive-date=October 4, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

The winners were announced at the award ceremony on March 29, 1989.<ref name=ChicagoTribuneOscars>{{cite news|last=Kehr |first=Dave |title='Rain Man' The Big Winner, But Upsets Put Zip In Oscars |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1989/03/30/rain-man-the-big-winner-but-upsets-put-zip-in-oscars/ |access-date=October 4, 2013 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=March 30, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131005034111/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1989-03-30/news/8903300960_1_61st-academy-awards-rain-man-screenplay-award |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Best Actress winner [[Jodie Foster]] became the eighth person in history to win the aforementioned category for a film with a single nomination. The last person to achieve this feat was [[Sophia Loren]] when she won for ''[[Two Women]]'' in [[34th Academy Awards|1961]]. Best Actor winner [[Dustin Hoffman]] was the fifth person to win the aforementioned category twice.<ref>{{cite news|url= http://goldderby.latimes.com/awards_goldderby/2009/02/oscar-news-411.html |title=Sean Penn is the ninth actor to win two lead Oscars |last=O'Neil |first=Tom |date=February 23, 2009 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=June 6, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130308055511/http://goldderby.latimes.com/awards_goldderby/2009/02/oscar-news-411.html |archive-date=March 8, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> [[Sigourney Weaver]] became the fifth performer to receive [[list of actors nominated for two Academy Awards in the same year|two acting nominations in the same year]]<ref name="APO">{{harvnb|Levy|2003|p=83}}</ref> but did not win in either category.<ref>{{harvnb|Levy|2003|p=283}}</ref> [[John Lasseter]] and  [[William Reeves (animator)|William Reeves]] won Best Animated Short Film for ''[[Tin Toy]]'', which was [[Pixar]]'s first Oscar ever and the first [[computer-generated imagery|CGI]] film to win an Oscar.<ref>{{cite book|last=Price|first=David|year=2008|title=The Pixar Touch|location=New York|publisher=[[Alfred A. Knopf]]|isbn=978-0-307-26575-3|ref=Price|page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780307265753/page/106 106]|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780307265753/page/106}}</ref>

*To the [[National Film Board of Canada]] in recognition of its 50th anniversary and its dedicated commitment to originate artistic, creative and technological activity and excellence in every area of film making.<ref>{{cite news|last=Solomon |first=Charles |title=Drawing Attention to Canada, Winning Oscars in the Process |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-mar-24-ca-12048-story.html |access-date=September 13, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 24, 2000 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131006121501/http://articles.latimes.com/2000/mar/24/entertainment/ca-12048 |archive-date=October 6, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

==The ceremony==
[[File:Allan Carr at 1989 Academy Awards.jpg|thumb|right|[[Allan Carr]] served as producer for the 61st Academy Awards.|alt=Photo of Allan Carr in 1989.]]
[[File:Amy Irving cropped.jpg|[[Amy Irving]] at the Governor's Ball after the Awards.|thumb]] 
In an attempt to attract viewers to the telecast and increase interest in the festivities, the Academy hired film producer and veteran Oscar ceremony executive talent coordinator [[Allan Carr]] to produce the 1989 ceremony.<ref>{{cite news |last= Williams|first=Jeannie|title=Twiggy's happy ending|work=[[USA Today]] |date=October 11, 1988 |page=2D|df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Volland |first=John |title=TV & Video |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-10-11-ca-3662-story.html |access-date=September 14, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=October 11, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131004232717/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-10-11/entertainment/ca-3662_1_la-cage-aux-folles |archive-date=October 4, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> In interviews with various media outlets, he expressed that it was a dream come true to produce the Oscars.<ref>{{cite news|last=Culhane |first=John |title=For Oscar's Producer, the Key Is C |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1989/03/26/movies/film-for-oscar-s-producer-the-key-is-c.html |access-date=October 4, 2013 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 26, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131005094552/http://www.nytimes.com/1989/03/26/movies/film-for-oscar-s-producer-the-key-is-c.html |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

Notable changes were introduced in the production of the telecast. For the first time, presenters announced each winner with the phrase "And the Oscar goes to..." rather than "And the winner is...".<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=11}}</ref> The green room where Oscar presenters, performers, and winners gathered backstage was transformed into a luxurious suite complete with furniture, pictures, refreshments, and other amenities called "Club Oscar".<ref>{{cite news|last=Uricchio|first=Marylynn|title=Awards show producer is putting posh on Oscar|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19890329&id=h9BRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7W0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=1941,8488003|access-date=October 4, 2013|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|date=March 29, 1989|page=12|df=mdy-all|archive-date=April 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418191008/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19890329&id=h9BRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=7W0DAAAAIBAJ&pg=1941,8488003|url-status=live}}</ref> Instead of hiring a host for the proceedings, Carr heavily relied on presenters, often grouped in pairs that had some connection, either through family or the film industry (a theme he billed as "couples, companions, costars, and compadres");<ref name="lamag snow job">{{cite web |last1=Hofler |first1=Robert |title=The Worst Oscars Ever |url=https://www.lamag.com/longform/snow-job/ |website=[[Los Angeles Magazine]] |access-date=23 January 2019 |date=1 March 2010 |df=mdy-all |ref=none |archive-date=January 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124102058/https://www.lamag.com/longform/snow-job/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005|p=5}}</ref><ref name="Siskel">{{cite news|last=Siskel |first=Gene |title=One Man's War Against The Dullest Night On Television |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1989/03/26/one-mans-war-against-the-dullest-night-on-television/ |access-date=October 5, 2013 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |date=March 26, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131006125425/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/1989-03-26/entertainment/8903290782_1_bob-werden-allan-carr-sciences-board |archive-date=October 6, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|last=Romero |first=Frances |title=No Hosts – Top 10 Worst Awards-Show Hosts |url= https://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0,28804,2055924_2055923_2055871,00.html |access-date=September 19, 2013 |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=March 1, 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130921061146/http://content.time.com/time/specials/packages/article/0%2C28804%2C2055924_2055923_2055871%2C00.html |archive-date=September 21, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> not until [[91st Academy Awards|2019]] would another ceremony lack a host.<ref name="keegan20190220">{{Cite news |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/features/politics-oscar-inside-academys-long-hard-road-a-hostless-show-1187424 |title=The Politics of Oscar: Inside the Academy's Long, Hard Road to a Hostless Show |last=Keegan |first=Rebecca |date=2019-02-20 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |access-date=2019-02-25 |language=en |df=mdy-all |archive-date=February 25, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190225041612/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/features/politics-oscar-inside-academys-long-hard-road-a-hostless-show-1187424 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Several other people were involved in the production of the ceremony. Jeff Margolis served as director of the telecast.<ref>{{cite web |title=Credits |url=http://jeffmargolisproductions.com/credits/ |publisher=Jeff Margolis Productions |access-date=October 4, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005000932/http://jeffmargolisproductions.com/credits/ |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all }}</ref> Lyricist and composer [[Marvin Hamlisch]] was hired as musical supervisor of the festivities.<ref>{{cite news |last=Voland |first=John |title=Movies |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-10-27-ca-267-story.html |access-date=October 24, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=October 27, 1988 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029223517/http://articles.latimes.com/1988-10-27/entertainment/ca-267_1_oscar-show |archive-date=October 29, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Comedian and writer [[Bruce Vilanch]] was hired as a writer for the broadcast, a role he filled until 2014.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Vary |first=Adam B. |title=An Oscar Insider Tells All |url= https://www.ew.com/article/2010/02/05/oscar-insider-tells-all |access-date=October 4, 2013 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |date=February 5, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150206101224/http://www.ew.com/article/2010/02/05/oscar-insider-tells-all |archive-date=February 6, 2015 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Carr had also rounded up eighteen young stars, including [[Patrick Dempsey]], [[Corey Feldman]], [[Ricki Lake]], and [[Blair Underwood]], to perform in a musical number entitled "I Wanna Be an Oscar Winner".<ref>{{harvnb|Pond|2005| p=8}}</ref> Unlike in most Oscar ceremonies, however, Carr announced that none of the three songs nominated for Best Original Song would be performed live.<ref name="Siskel"/>

The telecast was also remembered for being the final public appearance of actress and comedian [[Lucille Ball]], where she and co-presenter [[Bob Hope]] were given a standing ovation.<ref>{{cite news|title=Comedian Lucille Ball suffers a heart attack|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1314&dat=19890419&id=hLsyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zu8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=6799,3215179|access-date=October 5, 2013|work=[[The Spokesman-Review]]|date=April 19, 1989|df=mdy-all|archive-date=April 6, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230406021552/https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1314&dat=19890419&id=hLsyAAAAIBAJ&sjid=zu8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=6799,3215179|url-status=live}}</ref> On April 26, almost a month after the ceremony, she died from a [[dissecting aortic aneurysm]] at age 77.<ref>{{cite news|last=Flint |first=Peter B. |title=Lucille Ball, Spirited Doyenne of TV Comedies, Dies at 77 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/27/obituaries/lucille-ball-spirited-doyenne-of-tv-comedies-dies-at-77.html |access-date=October 5, 2013 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=April 27, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131006062842/http://www.nytimes.com/1989/04/27/obituaries/lucille-ball-spirited-doyenne-of-tv-comedies-dies-at-77.html |archive-date=October 6, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

===Opening number===
In an effort to showcase more glamour and showmanship in the ceremony, producer Carr hired playwright Steve Silver to co-produce an opening number inspired by Silver's long-running musical revue, ''[[Beach Blanket Babylon]]''.<ref name="SnowLowe">{{cite web |title=And the loser is... |url=http://theenvelope.latimes.com/awards/oscars/env-worstoscars27feb27,0,2820773,full.story |first=Steve |last=Pond |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=February 27, 2005 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131006034804/http://theenvelope.latimes.com/awards/oscars/env-worstoscars27feb27%2C0%2C2820773%2Cfull.story |archive-date=October 6, 2013 |df=mdy-all |ref=none |access-date=October 5, 2013 }}</ref> The segment consisted of an elaborate stage show centered on actress [[Eileen Bowman]], dressed as [[Snow White (Disney character)|Snow White]] from [[The Walt Disney Company|Disney's]] ''[[Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937 film)|Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs]]'', who comes to Hollywood and is entranced by its glamour.<ref name="SnowLowe"/> Like ''Beach Blanket Babylon'', the opening act also featured dancers wearing giant, elaborate hats.<ref name="SnowLowe"/> In a setting designed to resemble the [[Cocoanut Grove (Los Angeles)|Cocoanut Grove]] nightclub, Hollywood dignitaries such as actresses [[Alice Faye]], [[Dorothy Lamour]], [[Cyd Charisse]], her husband [[Tony Martin (American singer)|Tony Martin]], as well as [[Charles Rogers (actor)|Buddy Rogers]] and [[Vincent Price]] were prominently featured, while singer and television producer [[Merv Griffin]] sang a rendition of the song "[[I've Got a Lovely Bunch of Coconuts]]" (of which he had had a hit recording in 1949). Bowman and actor [[Rob Lowe]] then sang a reworked version of [[Creedence Clearwater Revival]]'s "[[Proud Mary]]", with lyrics rewritten to refer to the film industry.<ref name="SnowLowe"/>

===Critical reviews and public reaction===
The majority of media outlets panned the show. ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' television critic [[Howard Rosenberg]] lamented, "the Academy Awards telecast on [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] was surprisingly devoid of magic. It was on the musty side, and compared with [[31st Annual Grammy Awards|last month's Grammycast]], absolutely moribund."<ref>{{cite news|last=Rosenberg |first=Howard |title= Overcast for Allan Carr's Oscarcast |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-03-30-ca-1030-story.html |access-date=September 17, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 30, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005005937/http://articles.latimes.com/1989-03-30/entertainment/ca-1030_1_allan-carr |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Film critic [[Janet Maslin]] chastised the opening number, saying it "deserves a permanent place in the annals of Oscar embarrassments". She also bemoaned that the "I Wanna Be an Oscar Winner" number "was confusingly shot and inspired no confidence in Hollywood's future".<ref>{{cite news|last=Maslin |first=Janet |title= Review/Television; The Oscars as Home Entertainment |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1989/03/31/movies/review-television-the-oscars-as-home-entertainment.html |access-date=September 17, 2013 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=March 31, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131005012441/http://www.nytimes.com/1989/03/31/movies/review-television-the-oscars-as-home-entertainment.html |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> Television editor Tony Scott of ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' complained, "The 61st Annual Academy Awards extravaganza—seen in 91 different countries including, for the first time, the [[Soviet Union]]—turned out to be a TV [[wikt:nyet|nyet]]" He also observed that the "Break-Out Superstars number" looked like they were "cavorting around a giant Oscar as if it were the [[golden calf]]".<ref name="reviews">{{harvnb|Hofler|2010|p=416}}</ref>

The telecast also received a mixed reception from professionals within the show business industry. Talent agent [[Michael Ovitz]] praised Carr, saying that he had "brought show business back to the movie business". Actress [[Jennifer Jones]] thanked Carr in a written letter to the producer, which read, "You delivered."<ref>{{cite news|last=Champlin |first=Charles |title= Allan Carr: 'We Won the Town' |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-04-04-ca-1065-story.html |access-date= October 5, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=April 4, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131006065351/http://articles.latimes.com/1989-04-04/entertainment/ca-1065_1_allan-carr |archive-date=October 6, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> On the other hand, seventeen people, including actors [[Paul Newman]], [[Gregory Peck]], and [[Julie Andrews]], and directors [[Billy Wilder]] and [[Joseph L. Mankiewicz]], signed an open letter deriding the telecast as "an embarrassment to both the Academy and the entire motion picture industry".<ref>{{cite news|last= Speers |first=W. |title=Judge Orders James Brown's Autograph |url=http://articles.philly.com/1989-04-29/news/26146222_1_autograph-judge-orders-james-state-prison |access-date=September 17, 2013 |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |date=April 29, 1989 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131004221338/http://articles.philly.com/1989-04-29/news/26146222_1_autograph-judge-orders-james-state-prison |archive-date=October 4, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

Just outside the auditorium, on Jefferson Boulevard, a group of San Francisco [[drag queen]]s, calling themselves the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence stood in [[Mae West]] wigs and gowns, saying that they had come “to show our support for Allan Carr” for producing the first “''gay Oscars''.”<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schulman |first=Michael |title=Oscar Wars: A History of Hollywood in Gold, Sweat, and Tears |publisher=Harper Collins |year=2023 |isbn=9780062859051 |pages=260 |language=English}}</ref> There has been speculation that some of the blowback against the ceremony, which was the first produced by an [[coming out|openly gay]] person and which prominently featured a musical number based on a [[gay nightclub]] show, was [[homophobic]] in nature,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Little |first1=Becky |title=The Scathing Reaction to the Last Oscars With No Host |url=https://www.history.com/news/oscars-controversy-1989-proud-mary |website=[[History (U.S. TV network)|History]] |access-date=23 January 2019 |language=en |date=22 January 2019 |df=mdy-all |archive-date=January 24, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190124010123/https://www.history.com/news/oscars-controversy-1989-proud-mary |url-status=live }}</ref> although others, such as Bruce Vilanch and David Geffen, have challenged that assessment.<ref name="lamag snow job"/>

In addition, [[The Walt Disney Company]] filed suit against [[AMPAS]] for use of the likeness of Snow White.<ref>{{cite news |title=Disney Sues Over Use of Snow White at Oscars |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-03-31-me-749-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |first=Nina |last=Easton |date=March 31, 1989 |access-date=September 17, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130905213834/http://articles.latimes.com/1989-03-31/local/me-749_1_snow-white-character |archive-date=September 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> The lawsuit demanded unspecified damages for "copyright infringement, unfair competition, and dilution of business reputation".<ref name="SnowJob">{{cite news |last=Hofler |first=Robert |title=Snow Job |url=http://www.lamag.com/features/2010/03/01/snow-job |access-date=September 13, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles (magazine)|Los Angeles]] |date=March 1, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131005190927/http://www.lamag.com/features/2010/03/01/snow-job |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all|ref=none }}</ref> Academy President Richard Kahn immediately issued an apology to the studio, and the lawsuit was subsequently dropped.<ref>{{cite news|last=Vaughan |first=Vicki |title=Disney Accepts Apology, Drops Academy Suit |url= https://www.orlandosentinel.com/1989/04/07/disney-accepts-apology-drops-academy-suit/ |access-date=October 5, 2013 |work=[[Orlando Sentinel]] |date=April 7, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20131005225653/http://articles.orlandosentinel.com/1989-04-07/business/8904070295_1_walt-disney-academy-disney-snow |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

Bowman has claimed that she was made to sign a [[gag order]] the next day, prohibiting her from speaking to the press about her performance for the next 13 years. She finally spoke about it publicly in a 2013 interview, in which she described the performance as looking "like a gay [[bar mitzvah]]".<ref name="i was snow white">{{cite news|last=Abramovitch |first=Seth |title='I Was Rob Lowe's Snow White': The Untold Story of Oscar's Nightmare Opening |url= https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/oscars-rob-lowes-snow-white-422225 |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=February 20, 2013 |access-date=June 7, 2013 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130518013544/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/oscars-rob-lowes-snow-white-422225 |archive-date=May 18, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

===Ratings and aftermath===
Despite the criticism regarding the production of the ceremony, the American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 42.68&nbsp;million people over its length, which was a 1% increase from the [[60th Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref name="Oscar ratings">{{cite news |last=Gorman |first=Bill |title=Academy Awards Show Ratings |url=http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |access-date=September 5, 2013 |work=[[TV by the Numbers]] |publisher=[[Tribune Media]] |date=February 17, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131109025135/http://tvbythenumbers.zap2it.com/2009/02/17/academy-awards-show-ratings/12818/ |archive-date=November 9, 2013 |df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson |first=Greg |title=Call It the Glamour Bowl |url=https://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |access-date=September 14, 2013 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=March 18, 1999 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130928053918/http://articles.latimes.com/1999/mar/18/business/fi-18458/2 |archive-date=September 28, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> The show also drew higher [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 29.81% of households watching over a 50.41 share.<ref name="Oscar ratings"/> It was the highest-rated Oscar broadcast since the [[56th Academy Awards|56th ceremony]], held in 1984.<ref name="SnowJob"/> An estimated 75&nbsp;million total viewers watched all or part of the awards.<ref>{{cite news|title=Entertainment : 75 Million Watched Oscars on TV |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-03-30-mn-1075-story.html |access-date=April 26, 2026 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 30, 1989 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191211002631/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1989-03-30-mn-1075-story.html |archive-date=December 11, 2019 }}</ref>

Nevertheless, AMPAS created an Awards Presentation Review Committee to evaluate and determine why the telecast earned such a negative reaction from the media and the entertainment industry.<ref name="SnowJob"/> The committee later determined that Carr's biggest mistake was allowing the questionable opening number to run for 12 minutes. Producer and former [[Directors Guild of America]] president [[Gilbert Cates]], who headed the committee, said that Carr would not have received such harsh criticism if the number had been much shorter.<ref name="SnowJob"/> Cates was subsequently hired as producer of the [[62nd Academy Awards|succeeding year's telecast]].<ref name="Cates">{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=768}}</ref>

According to various showbiz insiders and reporters, the criticism and backlash from the ceremony resulted in Carr never again producing a film or theatrical show. He died from complications resulting from [[liver cancer]] on June 29, 1999, at the age of 62.<ref name="SnowLowe"/><ref name="SnowJob"/>

====Box office performance of nominees====
At the time of the nominations announcement on February 15, the combined gross of the five Best Picture nominees at the US box office was $188&nbsp;million, with an average of $37.7&nbsp;million per film.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars>{{cite news|title=1988 Academy Award Nominations and Winner for Best Picture |url=https://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1988&p=.htm |access-date=October 5, 2013 |work=[[Box Office Mojo]] |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131005101236/http://boxofficemojo.com/oscar/chart/?yr=1988&p=.htm |archive-date=October 5, 2013 |df=mdy-all}}</ref> ''Rain Man'' was the highest earner among the Best Picture nominees, with $97&nbsp;million in domestic box office receipts.<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/> The film was followed by ''Working Girl'' ($42.1&nbsp;million), ''The Accidental Tourist'' ($24.2&nbsp;million), ''Mississippi Burning'' ($18.6 million), and finally ''Dangerous Liaisons'' ($6.69&nbsp;million).<ref name=BoxOfficeOscars/>

Of the top 50 grossing movies of the year, 52 nominations went to 13 films. Only ''Big'' (3rd), ''Rain Man'' (5th), ''Working Girl'' (21st), ''The Accused'' (32nd), ''The Accidental Tourist'' (38th), ''Gorillas in the Mist'' (40th), ''Mississippi Burning'' (45th), and ''Tucker: The Man and His Dream'' (50th) were nominated for Best Picture, directing, acting, or screenwriting. The other top 50 box office hits that earned nominations were ''Who Framed Roger Rabbit'' (1st), ''Coming to America'' (2nd), ''Die Hard'' (7th), ''Beetlejuice'' (9th), and ''Willow'' (12th).
